newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea unveils steps to boost competitiveness.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea unveils steps to boost competitiveness.

text.p: South Korea's finance ministry announced new measures on Wednesday to boost the sagging economy, including slashing domestic steel prices and opening power production to private-sector competition.
A ministry statement also said the government would make it easier for big companies to borrow money from overseas.
The moves are part of a government drive to improve corporate competitiveness by bringing down costs.

Company profits are being slashed by plunging prices for South Korea's major exports. With no sign of any immediate recovery in prices of semiconductors, steel and petrochemical products, government planners are focusing on making industrial inputs cheaper and reducing the cost of funds.

"Structural weakness is the main cause of the current economic downturn," said Nam Sang-duck, director of the ministry's economic policy division. "It has become urgent to boost efficiency through cost-cutting and privatisation."

South Korea has forecast a $19 billion trade deficit this year, up from $10 billion last year, and has said the wider deficit will limit economic growth to about seven percent, compared to nine percent last year.

As part of the new measures, Pohang Iron and Steel Co (POSCO), which is 20 percent-owned by the government, will cut the domestic price of hot coiled steel this month by eight percent to 236,000 won ($284), the ministry said.

A POSCO official said the price cut would only apply to steel produced in the company's new electric-powered furnace, which is still in test operation but is expected to account for 15 percent of the company's output in 1997.
POSCO is the world's second-largest steel maker after Japan's Nippon Steel Corp
The ministry also said private companies would be allowed to compete with the state power monopoly, Korea Electric Power Corp (KEPCO), on non-nuclear power production.
However, KEPCO would retain its monopoly on power distribution, a ministry statement said.

Restrictions on large firms seeking overseas borrowings will be lifted if their purchases of locally-produced equipment in the previous year meet government requirements. Currently, only small- and medium-sized firms can access foreign loans to finance capital goods purchases.
The ministry said timetables for opening the power sector and easing borrowing restrictions would be announced later.

To reduce the cost of state goods and services, the government will freeze its budget for employee wages next year, the statement said. Savings will also come from laying off 10,000 state employees working under short-term employment contracts.
"We will also promote privatisation as much as possible, especially in the areas of medical services and management of port facilities," Nam said.

The ministry said the government would ease rules on new entries into the land freight transportation business. South Korean companies currently face the highest distribution costs among Asian nations, the statement said.
Brokers said they were disappointed that the package did not mention any easing in reserve requirement ratios for banks, a move that could bring down interest rates.

However, the ruling New Korea Party later announced that it had agreed in principle with economic planners that the ratios would be adjusted. The announcement lifted South Korea's stock index 2.53 percent to close at 817.78 points.
